subsubtopic: MR. REID-ATTENDANCE OF MEMBERS OF HOUSE OF COMMONS BEFORE SENATE COMMITTEES-RULING BY MR. SPEAKER
speechtext:
Order, please. On Wednesday, February 19, last the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Reid) rose on a question of privilege regarding the matter of members of this House appearing before committees of the other place to make representations to them on legislation which has gone through the stages of consideration in this chamber. The matter was raised subsequently and the question that was put by the hon. parliamentary secretary was whether a member can go to the other place and raise doubts about a piece of legislation on which this House of Commons has already taken a stand.
It seems to me that the hon. parliamentary secretary has raised two questions: first, can a member appear before a
committee of the other place? I suppose that amounts to a question of whether a member of this chamber can be prevented from so doing. On examining the precedents that were cited, and the Standing Orders, I can find nothing which bears directly upon the point of an hon. member of this House voluntarily appearing before a Senate committee. In any case, the precedents which would appear to offer some assistance are very early precedents which seem to me to have been overriden by usage common to the practices of this House since 1946, whereunder ministers have appeared in assistance of legislation and members have appeared in assistance of their own bills.
While exceptions are provided in this case under the Standing Orders of the other place, they are not referred to in the Standing Orders of this chamber. Accordingly, whatever precedents there were which might have supported the proposition that a member of this chamber could have been prevented from appearing before a committee of the other place seem to have been overridden by recent practices. Accordingly, I am not able to conclude that there is any authority whereunder the Chair could prevent such a thing being done by a member of this chamber.
The second question is whether, in so doing, a member can cast doubts upon legislation that has already been dealt with in this chamber. It seems to me that is hypothetical. No suggestion is made that such an event has taken place and no specific evidence of any occurrence is offered in support of such an allegation. In fact, no motion or inquiry seeking any action on the part of the Chair is appended to the hon. member's question of privilege. I would therefore conclude that no evidence is offered to support the contention that in any recent or specific case a breach of the privileges or Standing Orders of this House has taken place, and therefore I cannot find that a prima facie question of privilege is involved.
I should add, however, that much of the comment that was made in the course of the discussion-which was very long-on this very important point was valid. I refer, for example, to the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) to the effect that it is a curious anomaly that the other place takes such a grave view of this matter, sufficient to inscribe in its Standing Orders the punishment and penalties that ought to be visited upon one of its members who might condescend to come to this place and appear before this House or its emanations, but it takes a different attitude toward the presence of members of this chamber appearing before that chamber or its committees.
In addition, I am troubled by the fact that a committee of the other place having received, in any particular proceeding, one member of this chamber as a witness, it might find it most awkward to refuse others who wanted to

February 27, 1975
Public Service
appear. I cannot help but wonder if one day we may see this as a question of privilege of quite another form when a member or members-and, of course, they could be considerable in number-indicate that because one member of this House has appeared before a Senate committee to comment on legislation that has been passed by this House, surely that ought to be a privilege or a right extended to all other members who hold different views. While that would be action outside this chamber, it might pose a thorny question about the rights and privileges of members of this House.
Finally, from our own members' point of view it would seem to me that in doing so, obviously members are putting themselves in a situation where they are inviting a breach of Standing Order 35 which prohibits comment or reflection upon decisions of this House by members of this House, and they are inviting potentially grave affronts to parliament: they are inviting breaches of the privileges of the House. In fact, it seems to me that great care is needed on the part of hon. members appearing before committees of the other place in order to avoid these pitfalls. I can perhaps summarize these sentiments by saying it is to be hoped that neither members of this chamber nor of the other place will want to see that practice greatly encouraged.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED RESUMPTION OF NEGOTIATIONS WITH POSTAL EMPLOYEES-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I seek the unanimous consent of the House to discuss a matter of pressing and urgent necessity.
Considering that the federal government indicated last year that no layoff would result from the impact of technological changes on the postal system, and that, as reported in the press, 6,000 Toronto postal workers have just been laid off for the purpose of possibly crushing the strike of blue collar workers, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard):
That the House discuss this situation now, so that immediate corrective action may be taken to remedy this situation and create as soon as possible a climate truly favourable to meaningful bargaining in this area.

speechtext:
A question to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs. Considering that interest rates on mortgages are now in the neighbourhood of 11 per cent, I would like to ask the minister whether, following the decision by the government of
[Mr. MacKay.)
British Columbia recently to embark on a program which would provide mortgages at 6 per cent, the federal government would be willing to initiate a joint federal-provincial program with all the provinces which are interested in taking part to provide mortgages across the board to Canadians at 6 per cent?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subsubtopic: WILLINGNESS OF GOVERNMENT TO INITIATE FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL PROGRAM TO GRANT MORTGAGES AT 6 PER CENT
speechtext: I do not know whether the hon. member is aware of the fact that we have already made available an effective mortgage rate of 6 per cent for those Canadians who need it. proviso in each of these clauses by which certain subclauses would not take effect except by proclamation after April 15.
The two clauses to which I refer, namely, clauses 4 and 7, have caused great concern to the provincial governments and great anxiety to the oil companies and to the mining industry. They have also given rise to considerable opposition by hon. members in all parties on this side of the House. As the House knows, clause 4 provides that royalties paid to a provincial government in any form whatsoever are not deductible for income tax purposes. The minister has made it clear that royalties paid to private corporations, or royalties paid to a foreign government in cases where a Canadian firm is engaged in mining or petroleum production in other countries, will be admissible for income tax purposes. However, where royalties are paid to a provincial government they will not be deductible for income tax purposes.
Clause 7 contains a subclause dealing with fair market value. The result is that companies which are developing a non-renewable resource such as minerals, oil or gas will not be taxed on the basis of the price they receive for their products but on the basis of the price which is paid to the provincial government or any agency of the provincial government which sells those products. This looks to me and to my hon. friends like an attempt to prevent a provincial government from deciding how it will manage and market the resources of its province in a manner which it feels is most advantageous to the people to whom those resources rightfully belong.
It is the view of the members of this party that these two provisions in clauses 4 and 7 represent a serious and unwarranted intervention in an area of jurisdiction lying within the authority of the provincial governments. Under section 92 of the British North America Act, the resources of a province come within the exclusive jurisdiction of the province and the province has the right to determine the division of economic rent between the Crown in right of a province and the industry. The federal government has the right to tax the revenue which industry receives for exploiting and developing those resources. It also has the right to adjust the equalization payments so as to take into account revenue which the provincial government gets from the marketing of those resources.
But in this legislation the federal government has gone further and is seeking to intervene in deciding how a province chooses to manage its resources and how it shall decide to divide the economic rent between the provincial government and the industries engaged in resource development. This, in my opinion, is an act unprecedented in the history of Canada. Never before has a federal government sought to intervene in the field of resource development, in the field of royalties or with respect to the price a provincial government will get for the sale of products which belong to the people of that province.
I do not intend to deal, now, with the constitutional aspects of the matter. If the provincial governments decide that the federal government has exceeded its constitutional powers, it is a matter for them to determine whether or not to submit the question to the courts and it will be for the courts to decide the issue. There is, however, a political aspect to this whole question raised by these two clauses.

This country has to decide between the concept of co-operative federalism or confrontation federalism. The first prime minister of Canada, Sir John A. Macdonald, said that this was not an easy country to govern. That remark will probably go down in Canadian political history as the greatest understatement ever made.
It is well known that Sir John A. Macdonald would have preferred, initially, to see a unitary form of government. As events transpired, we developed a federal system, and I think most of us are convinced that this was probably the right decision for the Fathers of Confederation to make. It is true that there are some advantages in a unitary form of government, but it is equally true that in a federal system of government the advantages, at least in my opinion, far outweigh the disadvantages. In a country of such vast space, with a people extending from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean, there is a great deal to be said for having governments that are close to the people, in having governments that take over areas of jurisdiction such as health and welfare, education, resource development, labour laws and agriculture; matters which can be, I think experience has shown, much better administered on a provincial basis than by a unitary form of government which is operated from Ottawa.
Sometimes you get some very good provincial governments, too.

However, as experience has shown, there arise differences of opinion with respect to the exercise of the respective responsibilities given to the two levels of government. Conflicts have arisen in the past and undoubtedly conflicts will arise in the future. We have to decide how these conflicts are to be resolved. They can be resolved by confrontation, by taking cases to the courts, and by building up hostility in which the people of Canada are torn between the claims of their provincial government and the claim of the government of Canada.
But there have been a surprising number of instances in our history where federal and provincial governments have been able to resolve their differences and reach consensus in settling conflicts. This has been true in the case of pension legislation, welfare legislation, health legislation. Solutions have been worked out in regard to labour legislation and in the particularly difficult field of agricultural legislation, where the federal government has responsibility for marketing and the provincial government for production. These differences in points of view have been worked out by compromise and negotiation and a solution has been found.
The energy crisis which began in the latter part of 1973 has raised a whole new area of possible conflict and confrontation arising from the fact that the provincial governments have the right to set the price of products such as oil and gas, or the price of a specific mineral, whereas the federal government has jurisdiction in dealing with these products when they cross interprovincial and international boundaries.

For that reason we supported the minister last year when he sought to keep the price of oil, for example-this is equally true of copper, wheat and other commodities-at a level that was fair and commensurate with the economic situation in this country.
Nevertheless, it was not an easy conflict to resolve. The premiers of the provinces which produce oil took the position that they had the right to set the price of a barrel of oil, a depleting resource; that they had the right to build up reserves against future requirements to explore for further resources and to develop new industries when the oil had been completely depleted. Consequently, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) called a first ministers' conference which was held last March. At that conference some fear was expressed that the premiers, particularly of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, might take the position that, irrespective of what the federal government did about interprovincial or international prices, they would set the price of their oil and that if they did not get that price they would withhold production.
That would have been a serious step to take, and it is to the everlasting credit of the premiers that they did not take that position. At the conference with the Prime Minister in March, 1974, they agreed to accept the price of $6.50 a barrel. The Prime Minister praised them for their co-operation and assistance in working out a compromise that appeared to be reasonably satisfactory to all concerned. The premiers went back to their respective provinces convinced that this was to be the situation until at least June of 1975, and that they could count on this agreement being carried through.
This House is now confronted with a piece of legislation that projects us into an entirely new ball-game. Naturally, the provinces feel, to put it in the bluntest terms, that they have been double-crossed. They also point out that they, in their turn, have kept their share of the bargain. Premier Barrett of British Columbia announced that he was going to raise the export price of gas on January 1, 1975. At the request of the Prime Minister, he agreed not to raise the price of gas until after the first ministers' conference. He was prepared to be co-operative and to let this matter rest until all the premiers and the federal government had had an opportunity to review the situation.
This is why Premier Blakeney of Saskatchewan wired the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) on February 18 and asked him to hold back clause 4 and clause 7 until after the first ministers' conference. It is why members of the committee of the whole during the last two or three days have been pleading with the minister to put a provision in both those clauses stipulating that certain subclauses would not come into effect except by proclamation after April 15.
However, the federal government has refused to do this and we are now confronted with a piece of legislation which enables the Prime Minister to go to the first minis-

ters' conference in April with a fait accompli. He will say to them, "Parliament has decided: I no longer have any choice in the matter. This is how we are going to handle resources. This is how we propose to interfere in the management and disposition of the resources of the provinces. The only resort you have is if you want to take the matter to the courts and have a long, protracted constitutional argument".
I think this a good time for members of this House to realize how fragile the federal system is. I think it a good time for members to realize that a country which faces as many problems as Canada does at present, needs all the good will and all the co-operation it can get from all the levels of government. This is true in many fields. The Minister of Finance, in tackling both unemployment and inflation effectively and aggressively, will need the cooperation of the provincial governments.
Also, the energy question will still be before us. If Canada finally becomes a signatory to the international energy agreement, which may under certain circumstances call for a restriction on consumption of petroleum products in this country, we will need the co-operation of the provincial governments. If in the situation which is likely to confront us in the next few months and the next few years there is an atmosphere of hostility, with the federal government using the big club and the provincial premiers being angry and annoyed, I think federalism will not work as effectively as it should.
It is only natural for disagreement to occur from time to time between federal and provincial authorities. Naturally, they will not always agree as to the exact areas of their jurisdiction, particularly where they overlap. But the hallmark of statesmanship is for the federal government to retain sufficient good will so that it can prevent hostility and alienation from making impossible a co-ordinated approach to the national problems which confront Canada at this time.
Over the years that I have been in public life I have seen at first-hand many instances where previous federal administrations have been able to bring about that kind of co-operation and co-ordination to meet situations in which conflict and hostility could easily have arisen. The test of statesmanship will be this government's capacity to attain national objectives while at the same time securing the co-operation and good will of the provincial governments with whom it must work, which in most cases will be forthcoming if the federal government adopts an attitude of conciliation and good will.
I propose to move an amendment, because I believe that a solution can be found. The Minister of Finance, and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources will agree with me, I think, when I say that so far as my colleagues and I are concerned, we have never tried to play-off federal and provincial interests. It is comparatively easy for any politician to play-off the federal government against his province or local region. We have repeatedly stood by the federal government when it has said that the national interest must come first. But the national interest can only come first if the federal government is able to persuade the governments of the provinces and the people of the
February 27, 1975

provinces to believe that the federal government is doing this in a fair and equitable manner and not by getting out the big club or riding roughshod over the provinces.
I say to the Minister of Finance that of course the government can use its majority to pass Bill C-49, amending the Income Tax Act, through this House. This the government can do by virtue of its political muscle. But the Minister of Finance and the government must recognize that it is possible to win the battle but to lose the war, and in the long run it is more important to win the war against economic stagnation, against inflation and against national disunity than it is to win a battle which in the long run could be self-defeating.
Therefore, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That Bill C-49 be not now read a third time but that it be referred back to the committee of the whole House for the purpose of reconsidering clause 4 and clause 7 thereof.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few remarks before this extremely important bill is given third reading. I am told that credit unions are awaiting this legislation impatiently. I am aware of that, Mr. Speaker, but 1 also know that the provinces are awaiting impatiently the result of today's vote. I hope they will be favourable to upholding those provincial jurisdictions we stood for so proudly on this side of the House, as did for that matter the hon. member who spoke for me.
Mr. Speaker, we are definitely going to support that amendment as it meshes with our approach based on respect for provincial rights and provincial jurisdictions.
There are two founding nations in this country.

Yes, there are two founding nations in this country. It was just pointed out to me, Mr. Speaker. Several immigrants also came here to help us build this beautiful country that is Canada, a country that nevertheless still has its problems.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few more comments on Bill C-49. In view of its importance, I am pleased to participate in the last minutes of this debate. As all hon. members, I recognize of course that this bill is quite important for all Canadians and affects all sectors of the taxation area. I recognize that it makes certain benefits available to several thousands of Canadians, and provides the government with necessary funds.
As several comments were made on those very important points, I would like nevertheless to make a few remarks on that clause designed to prevent from now on resource companies from deducting royalties paid to the provinces from their taxable incomes. I think that up until now, Mr. Speaker, several provinces indicated their opposition in that respect. The hon. member who spoke before me pointed that out by moving an amendment, and it is regrettable that the government remained inflexible on the recommendations of the provinces.
I would have thought, Mr. Speaker, that we would answer in the affirmative, that we would wait at the very
Income Tax
least until after the federal-provincial conference which will take place very soon, in order to allow the provinces to discuss that very important point. And the question is why this government refuses to defer those particular clauses affecting the provinces in order to allow them to discuss those powers which this government is granting itself in this bill. Recently, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) unequivocally stated that the provisions on royalties are final and will not be the subject matter of negocia-tions at the next federal-provincial conference. I regret to be induced to believe that this is an unacceptable centralizing scheme and I think it is important for members to discuss this matter reasonably and objectively this afternoon.
That is the important point of this bill. We can be accused to oppose a legislation which is hardly advantageous as I said earlier, but I believe that the striking feature of the whole bill is that centralizing attitude.
We heard a good deal about viable, profitable federalism. How could we achieve such an objective by introducing a bill unacceptable to the provinces? It could be suggested that it is for the sake of national unity that we passed this legislation. The hon. member who spoke before me raised that point. I believe that if it is in the national interest, we should respect in fact the provincial jurisdiction recognized in our constitution. Then, I say we could speak of provocation and arrogance against the provinces. Undoubtedly, the premiers or the responsible ministers who will meet in the near future will not be prepared to have objective discussions with the federal government.
I should have thought that the federal government has the responsibility for coordinating the efforts of the provinces. We know full well that the provinces, in their own spheres, are making great efforts to solve the problems of their electors. To my mind, it does not behoove the federal government to centralize, and to take unilateral decisions such as the one it is now taking.
In view of the stand taken by the federal government, through which it will be depriving the provinces of considerable income, I say it is "holding-up" the provinces in broad daylight.
Perhaps, I should at this point put this question to hon. members: What are we doing about our responsibilities? Are we going to betray the people in this way? I hope not, Mr. Speaker. We must reflect on that aspect of the matter, and take into account the objections of the provinces to the clauses of the bill they consider unacceptable.
As for those who talk about national interest and the implementation of a workable federal system, I think their attitude only contributes to undermine our system. We discourage the provinces. As I said, they are making efforts considering the increasing number of problems within their respective territories. I also repeat that the federal government's basic responsibility is to co-ordinate rather than to centralize. I deeply regret that most government members have not been successful in urging their own government to respect the wish expressed by the provinces.
The federal government surely needs funds to run' the country, but I do not think it should assume alone that responsibility. In my opinion, when it comes to depriving

February 27, 1975
Income Tax
the provinces of certain taxing privileges or sums of money, I am convinced that provincial first ministers act in good faith. I believe that they would agree with their federal counterpart to give the federal government a fair share of the profits they derive from their natural resources. However, I repeat that it is unacceptable that a decision be made in Ottawa without consulting the provinces. This is definitely not the way we shall conceive a workable federal system, and we shall not as long as the provinces do not feel perfectly at ease within the present system.
I know that similar remarks have been made on several occasions. The failure of the government to listen carefully to the claims of the provinces always makes me sad. There again, we know for a fact that the provinces put forward some claims with regard to the coming federal-provincial meeting, but Parliament is being required and urged to pass this bill which infringes upon very important provincial jurisdictions.
So, as I said, decisions are made here in Ottawa without any consultation and then the provinces are asked to discuss the problems we are now facing. I wonder whether that is not a strange consultation to have before a decision is made.
Later on, one will wonder what happens either in the province of Quebec or in Alberta or in British Columbia. One will wonder why some provinces are not satisfied, why certain provinces are putting in so many claims to the Ottawa government, why we have those pitched battles between the federal government and the provinces.
We of the Progressive Conservative Party will be accused of concentrating our efforts on protecting Alberta's interests.
For once I was very happy to support the claims laid by Alberta's government which was carefully protecting its provincial rights. It was not only a responsibility, on its part, but a duty to protect the rights it has acquired a long time ago.
I think one could also ponder on what is going on in Quebec, on the thousands of Quebecers who are gradually losing faith in this federalism that is being called profitable or viable. Attitudes such as the one shown by this government are things that discourage not only the provincial premiers or the ministers responsible in that field but also the electors in every province. We still have the opportunity to think seriously about what we are going to do this afternoon. Either we say yes to the provinces and show our respect for provincial jurisdictions or, on the contrary, we say to the provinces that everything must be settled in Ottawa. And then we ask them to embrace the system, to have a feeling of freedom.
I venture to think, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members will assume their responsibility, which is not necessarily to support a political party or to see if it could be defeated or not in the House. I think that every member has formally committed himself to serve his constituents' interests at every opportunity. I think that today, we have a unique opportunity to serve the interests of the provinces without prejudice to the national interest.

Then, at the last minute, I appeal for much more understanding and open-mindedness than were shown until now with regard to certain clauses of the bill that are sure to displease the provinces if this legislation is passed.
This government had promised us a just society and started consultations. I hope they will meet their commitments much more honestly than they are doing presently.

I would have liked to know if, like many others, he intends to replace the Quebec first minister, because there are little problems at present. I did not suggest, Mr. Speaker, that it is because I belong to the Progressive Conservative party. I said that the duty of a Quebec member in particular, and of all members in general, was to respond to the needs of their province.
And I repeat, members who support the legislation as introduced will betray the interests of their own province. Recommendations made by the Quebec government do not favour the clauses now before us, because they feel the latter do not meet provincial needs.
Therefore, I wish I had seen Quebec members show their respect for provincial jurisdictions, or at least ask the minister in charge to wait until after the federal-provincial conference, in order to try and reach a solution satisfactory to the provinces.
I believe the federal government is in error if it believes it can decide alone in such matters. I repeat it is important that consultations be held before the federal-provincial conference. I believe that after, provinces will be quite ready to give the federal government a certain percentage of resource revenues because I believe the premiers are quite capable of assessing federal needs, in consultation with the federal representatives. I say however that if the federal government acted in this way, this is a unilateral and unacceptable decision.
Because I invite hon. members to examine this aspect, all types of arguments will be raised to lead people to believe that I am the only one who thinks he has got the truth. Mr. Speaker, this is absolutely not the case but, as a member of Parliament, I say that our responsibility is to respond to the hopes of the provinces when we speak of promoting proper federalism and ensuring its continuity. The way decisions are taken in this House will certainly not satisfy the provinces and help them rely on federalism.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I will again invite my colleagues in this House to think well before taking a vote on such a fundamental principle. I believe that a negative answer rejecting my call would not be forgiven by Canadian people; for they are anxious that the jurisdictions granted to the provinces under the constitution should be recognized, jurisdictions which could be totally quashed by this legislation. I believe that we have to look far ahead to understand the importance of this legislation and its implications not only on oil, but also on all areas of resources. I think that every member in his province must think it over to give an affirmative vote and allow the provinces to maintain the rights they have had for such a long time.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member for Joliette allow a question?
Yes.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the member for Joliette if the advantages which he referred to earlier in his speech and which Quebec got through an agreement on oil with Alberta and the other provinces were to bring the same profit to Quebecers, would he oppose them?

If I understand well, the hon. member asked me if I am going to vote against the legislation. I

will certainly do so. I am going to vote for the amendment because we are going to vote on an amendment requiring the federal government to allow the provinces to negotiate on royalties before accepting this piece of legislation.
And I think this is quite important. I said at the outset that this bill contained very good proposals, but one is unacceptable and cannot be supported by a member who honours his commitments.

Mr. Speaker, we are nearing the end of this debate, but I think there are a few things still to be said. In effect, we are debating the economic condition of the country for the first time in almost two years. I suggest the last budget is a rerun of the May budget, although conditions have changed since then. The May budget was concerned with attacking the resource industries and bringing their profits into the federal treasury, and also attacking the provinces on provincial rights. Both budgets have much in common, although the May budget imposed some conditions on the resource industries which were withdrawn in the November budget.
At the moment, the taxes on the resource industries will seriously cripple them and our economy for the next few years unless further changes are made. This attack was a direct violation of the principle of confederation whereby the provinces would own the resources and the people of the provinces would have the right to enjoy the revenues accruing from those resources. We have heard much about the rights of the provinces, and it is generally considered by students of the federal-provincial situation that the provinces have had decreasing taxation in the last few years, with increased commitments in the fields of health, welfare and social services. It is true that most of the increase is due to the actions of the federal government and it is hard to understand why there would be such action without consultation with the provinces.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has made the play that he is the saviour of national unity. There is no doubt that this has sharpened, particularly in western minds, the feeling that they are remote from Ottawa and that the federal government has no rapport with the provinces, particularly the west.
The November budget represents a partial withdrawal in the field of resources but leaves much to be desired in taxation of the oil and gas industries. The president of the Mining Association of Canada said recently that mining firms can expect at least two years of tough times. The mining industry depends greatly on sales to the United States and has felt the effects of the recession in that country. The president of the Mining Association of Canada was also pessimistic about the future of the resource industry because of the squeeze as between the federal and provincial tax systems. He said, as reported in the Montreal Gazette of February 27, 1975:
If you find anything, you couldn't justify developing it, so there's no use going out and looking.
He also said that federal and provincial taxes combined now range between 60 per cent and 130 per cent of profits.

February 27, 1975
Income Tax
The budget has not paid sufficient heed to Canada's worsening trade position. Last year our trade deficit went up from $6.6 billion, the 1973 figure, to $9.5 billion. Our high tariff walls and advantages given to the manufacturing industry and processors, by reduced taxation have not reversed the situation. But for the surplus of $5.5 billion in our crude materials trade last year, our trade position would be much more serious. Last year this country experienced a favourable balance of trade in petroleum to the extent of $1.5 billion. According to recent forecasts, our net trading deficit in petroleum products in the coming year will be $750 million. Yet it has been this government's policy to inflict punitive taxes on the oil and gas industry, thus diminishing activity in the search for oil and gas at the very time when such activity should be greatly increased.
By introducing the present budget, the federal government has decided to play fast and loose with our economy in an attempt to break the hold of the provinces, particularly the western provinces, in the field of resource taxation. We can only lose in the short run. The whole of Canada stands to lose much from this move. External forces are reducing the demand for our resources. Trade with Japan is not increasing as was hoped by trade officials who had forecast a $1 million increase in trade with that country. Japan wants to cut back by 30 per cent, purchases of Canadian copper. Copper represents our single most important export to Japan. This country is no longer considered as a reliable supplier of rapeseed and farm produce, and we shall lose markets because of strikes and shipping troubles. We have always tended to think that resources will fetch high prices and be in great demand, but the high prices of our resources on world markets are probably largely the result of devaluation of our currency.
The budget has failed to take into account the difficulties our exporters face in external markets. Further, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) refused the opposition's request for a modest reduction in income tax. Such a reduction would have left more money in the hands of wage earners and thus increased demand for durable goods, sales of which are falling off. The demand for cars and appliances is also soft, and more money in the hands of wage earners and taxpayers would stimulate sales. A modest reduction in income tax would also reduce the government's tendency to spend and institute new programs. Also, it would contribute to savings on the part of taxpayers, something that is vital to our economy. As well, a tax reduction would provide some insurance against renewed inflation which according to some forecasts is to increase markedly at the end of this year.
The thrust of this budget is in the wrong direction. Producers should be given more tax leeway so they can reinvest in more efficient and expansive growth. The government has already done this for manufacturers but has not permitted resource producers to be efficient and productive. Governments, federal and provincial, have taxed resources too heavily. They have failed to appreciate that much of the so-called increase in profits has been the result of inflation. Although we may not like it, we must be painfully aware that as a nation we would be foolish to depend on the manufacturing industry to provide us with a high standard of living-a high standard brought about

by external trade. Like it or not, Canada's primary industries, including agriculture, forestry and resources, have not been encouraged by this budget.

that I speak on third reading. It being his wish, I will make one of my rare speeches in the House to remind him of some of the facts that have been brought to the attention of parliament and are now reported in Hansard as the result of the debate that has taken place on Bill C-49. Having said that, I should like to direct a question to the government House leader and ask how he was so successful in silencing 107 of his backbenchers who must have wished to speak during committee of the whole stage on this bill, yet they sat mute throughout the entire deliberations.
Hear, hear!

I say that because surely it is strange, when we are considering income tax legislation and budgetary measures which will result in the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) taxing Canadians at the rate of $100 million a day, that the backbenchers sitting on the government side would have not been more anxious to participate in the committee of the whole review of the legislation on which we will soon have a third reading vote. I say that because we in the official opposition believe that government spending has got out of control with this government.
The spending spree that has occurred since the present Minister of Finance took office is truly remarkable. In the short period that he has been Minister of Finance the real growth in the country has been only 15 per cent but inflation has been 30 per cent. Government spending, however, has jumped 67 per cent, the money supply is up 56 per cent and credit and bank borrowings are up 82 per cent. Surely it is clear from these figures that this minister has far exceeded the economic excesses of his predecessor, Mr. Benson. Under Mr. Benson, a former minister of finance, inflation in the country was only 11.5 per cent, compared to inflation under this minister of 30 per cent. But, most significantly, spending under this Minister of Finance is up 95 per cent, based on his budgetary figures. In a similar previous period, spending under Mr. Benson was up 49 per cent.
We have made two main thrusts during debate on this bill. The first is that we believe the government can, and should, give a further tax reduction to Canadian taxpayers.
Hear, hear!

We believe such a reduction would result not only in the taxpayer having more money-and I would suggest he can spend his money better than this government can spend it for him-but it would also mean that this government might be restrained in its spending habits. If this government does not choose to discipline its spending, surely at some stage it is up to parliament to begin disciplining it in that respect.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, our second main thrust was that we believe the royalty taxation provisions in this bill are most unfortunate.

Calamitous!

We believe it is using a legislative means- a revenue, taxation means-to really distort the constitution of this country. We believe there are serious infringements of provincial rights within this bill. Many of our speakers, including my colleague the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), pointed out the difficulties which will arise. The hon. member for Joliette pointed out the position with respect to Quebec. I reiterate that we as an opposition are diametrically opposed to the revenue approach the minister has shown in this bill with respect to royalties.
We are anxious that the bill be proceeded with. We believe we have had a good debate. I am, frankly, disappointed that in debating the bill-which contains 142 sections and is 302 pages long-we have not had more participation from government backbenchers who must be as disturbed as we are by many of the provisions of this bill. But obviously the whip was out and they were silenced. As a result, some of those hon. members have told me privately that they know amendments will have to be made to the bill, yet they did not feel they could stand up and point out the amendments they believe will be needed.
Shame.

We are at the conclusion of this debate. I sincerely hope that although the Minister of Finance has walked roughshod over our suggestions to date, he will at least take our arguments into account and act in a more restrained way in future.

subsubtopic: LETTER FROM MINISTER OF JUSTICE TO SECRETARY OF STATE RESPECTING GRANT TO WOMEN'S GROUP
speechtext:
That an order of the House do issue for a copy of a letter written by the Minister of Justice to the Secretary of State, dated October 21, 1974, about a grant to a women's group in Saskatoon.
He said: Mr. Speaker, obviously this debate is not about the highly emotionally charged issue of abortion. The reason I wanted a copy of a letter from the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) which was leaked to the newspapers- a letter he wrote to the Secretary of State about a proposed grant to a women's group in Saskatoon-was to underline the whole issue of secrecy in government. I believe the leak was a calculated one. I believe that leaks of government information occur largely because of the very restrictive techniques the government uses in classification of documents.
I strongly believe that the system of classification referring to "Secret", "Top secret", "For eyes only", "This letter is a judicial opinion" or "is giving a legal opinion", and so on, is a technique to frustrate the free flow of information from parliament, ministers, and so on, to the public. In the few minutes available to me I hope to develop this theme.
Someone in the government-I wish I knew who it was, because I want to pay tribute to him personally-made a comment in another forum. It was made at the time when parliament was considering what to do about continuing the Canadian contribution to NATO. One of the documents the government used for basing its decision on was marked "Secret: for Canadian eyes only", and some wag on the government benches said that this admonition was for all Canadians except members of parliament. I think this rather hard-hearted statement underlines the much more fundamental problem which faces us as legislators. Here was a decision being made, the document was classified, a parliamentary committee was considering the whole issue, the document itself was for Canadian eyes only-officials and ministers-but the committee of this House charged with the responsibility of making recommendations to the government on the NATO issue could not see the document.
Then we consider the whole issue of papers prepared for the government and its departments by a consultant hired from outside the government service. I think last year's estimates included several hundred million dollars in consultants' fees. My inaccuracy is showing, but it was certainly a very large amount of money.

subsubtopic: LETTER FROM MINISTER OF JUSTICE TO SECRETARY OF STATE RESPECTING GRANT TO WOMEN'S GROUP
speechtext:
Three quarters of a billion.
February 27.1975

subsubtopic: LETTER FROM MINISTER OF JUSTICE TO SECRETARY OF STATE RESPECTING GRANT TO WOMEN'S GROUP
speechtext:
Yes, it was astronomical. My leader reminds me that it was three quarters of a billion dollars. That was the figure I had in my mind. It was so exorbitant that my simple maritime mind could not grasp the implications of spending such a vast amount of money on consulting fees. In most cases the papers and documentation produced by these outside consultants are not available to members of parliament. I think the spokesman of the minister is ready to take a very narrow view on this issue and use the technical expression that the letter to the Secretary of State was a legal opinion. I think this is indeed a narrow technical view.
I wish to now develop a couple of other thoughts about the whole issue of availability of documents and the secrecy in which government seems to wrap itself. In an article entitled "On telling people" which is to be found in Essays on Reform, 1967, which is edited by Bernard Crick, Professor J. A. G. Griffith writes:
The wish to take the lid off the machinery of government, to see how it works, who says what to whom, at what level decisions are taken, what private criteria are used, how far "politics" is allowed to override those criteria, on what statistical and other "facts" the decisions are based: this wish does not derive only from curiosity or from party animosity but also from self-interest, from quis custodiet, and from a feeling-by some-that governments represent another group interest.
Professor Griffith makes some suggestions that I will paraphrase for the purpose of this debate. First, we should be told much more about the background against which decisions are taken. Second, there is a vast, shaded area about which most of us know nothing and generally suspect the worst: flitting in and out of this are those who wish to appear to be of the number in the know. The nearer we are to the source of the truth, the more we will hear-although not necessarily the more truths. Obviously, foreign affairs and national defence are deepest in this shadow that Professor Griffith enunciates. We accept, obviously-who would not accept it-the need for some of this, but surely it is overdone.
Third, when the government consults private interests before finally taking decisions, could we not be told something of the bargains struck, the compromises reached, the promises given? We have an excellent example of this in the very tough decisions that obviously must be taken by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) on the matter of the severe problems faced by Canadian textile workers and their industry. Obviously, the government will be striking bargains with other governments and with that trade; yet the House, which at some time will have an obligation to make decisions based on those bargains, will know nothing about the background on which they were made.

subsubtopic: LETTER FROM MINISTER OF JUSTICE TO SECRETARY OF STATE RESPECTING GRANT TO WOMEN'S GROUP
speechtext: We will be in the same position as the minister.

subsubtopic: LETTER FROM MINISTER OF JUSTICE TO SECRETARY OF STATE RESPECTING GRANT TO WOMEN'S GROUP
speechtext:
Fourth, governments could afford to be much more open about their policies. Ministers seem to be genuinely fearful of being specific about the ends they are seeking to achieve. The Minister of Justice, because he also represents a constituency embracing part of the city of Saskatoon, wrote a letter to the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner). Somehow, in the great system of government,
Government Information
that letter was classified; at least, I could not get it in the ordinary course of events and must take up the time of the House to debate this motion.
I repeat, the issue is not that of abortion or the Criminal Code. A decision was taken by this parliament on that issue. Rather, the issue is whether parliament can obtain an important letter written by one minister to another on a current, topical issue, rather than have the letter leaked to the press because of the frustrations felt by the people- presumably they were servants of the Crown-who made it available to the press.
Professor Griffith ends with a plea for "telling people". Although the article was written for British readers I suggest it is equally apt in this country. We read in the newspapers, we listen to and look at political commentators, we hear ministerial statements and we are conscious of the existence of another world, the other side of the moon. So we become cynical to the point of switching off radio and television during general election broadcasts because, simply, we do not believe what is being said. I think this is crucial to the parliamentary institution. It is a curious fact, Mr. Speaker, that just on Monday of this week the Trilateral Commission attempted to convene a conference on the governability of democracy. It is somewhat ironical that the conference could not be held because of the public service strike which meant there was doubt whether guests from all over the world could get here. However, that irony could be discussed on another occasion.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I am flattered that the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) is in his seat this afternoon. He and I have been part of this debate since we entered this House 13 years ago. I think we have probably looked at all the same articles and we have come across a rather perceptive little book, written by Professor Brian Champman, called British Government Observed in which he says that the passion for secrecy is a phenomenon that is inherited from Great Britain: it had its origin in the days of Napoleon when the British government was anxious to keep unto itself its secrets.

subsubtopic: LETTER FROM MINISTER OF JUSTICE TO SECRETARY OF STATE RESPECTING GRANT TO WOMEN'S GROUP
speechtext: I think the Irish have to accept some responsibility.

subsubtopic: LETTER FROM MINISTER OF JUSTICE TO SECRETARY OF STATE RESPECTING GRANT TO WOMEN'S GROUP
speechtext:
My leader mentions the Irish. It is not yet St. Patrick's Day, so I will allow him to make that interpretation. I take the presence of the Postmaster General as encouragement. He sits close to where I am and I have heard him make pretty well the same plea that I make; that is, lessen the incessant secrecy. When I was in Washington recently, for example, somebody told me that the number of classified documents in the possession of the United States of America is so monumental that easy retrieval has become impossible. Classification, of course, is therefore a joke. Mere numbers have looked after the secrecy. There are hundreds of millions of documents in a huge warehouse in Virginia and it is terribly hard to obtain access to them because of the very number.
I suggest the truth is that if anything useful and significant is to be done in this free society, it must be done publicly and in such a way as to consult, involve and carry with it those affected. I suggest this is the core of some of our frustration and the reason people are convening semi-
28996-26/2

February 27, 1975
Government Information
nars on whether democracies are governable. The government has the responsibility, as parliamentarians have, of carrying the public with it when tough decisions should be taken. If every time we attempt to take the public along with us in this decision-making we are faced with "Classified", "This is a judicial opinion", "For eyes only" or "Top secret", it seriously impedes the work we are called upon to do. Understanding and consent in this instance does not spring from some previous interaction of government and voter at a general election but, I suggest, has to be the constantly renewed product of a continual exchange of communications. This is a stage where the two uglies-I have used the words before-of dehumanization and depersonalization make it more important than ever that legislators should understand the thrust and purpose of government policies and thus are able to communicate them to the public.
I am sorry I have taken so much time. I suggest it is not sufficient to keep repeating-I am guilty of this as well- with boring regularity slogans like "open access" or "executive privilege." We must avoid more than mere sloganeering. We must avoid what Harold Laski once described as the "trained incompetence of the specialist", that narrowness of vision which often comes with immersion in a program or a policy field. Breadth of view must be combined with technical skill in effective policy-making. Generally, the training of information technologists does not overcome their limited social and political sensitivities. That should be particularly true of members of parliament, otherwise every one of the 264 members of this House could sit in his office and never go to Halifax, Nanaimo or any point in between and become immersed in some issue. The danger is that specialists may never hear from elected representatives about the realities of those very decisions which must be made and about how those decisions will affect the specialists themselves.
I am the last man to stand here and criticize the public service. I will not repeat the oft stated compliments. I think our public service is excellent, but I think the best public servants recognize the need for a continual flow of information from what the poet calls "the heartland of this country", because that is where the hang-ups are and where the problems are to be found. We need a process of continuous interchange. Our quest for information is not helped by a very much exaggerated classification system.
My notice of motion really has little to do with the copy of a letter. The letter was made public to the press, because somebody in the minister's office leaked it. I have spent my time pleading for the government to be much more forthright in giving information. If information is given, I suggest there will be much greater public acceptance of some of the policies of the government, and presumably this is what the government devoutly wishes.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gilles Marceau (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subsubtopic: LETTER FROM MINISTER OF JUSTICE TO SECRETARY OF STATE RESPECTING GRANT TO WOMEN'S GROUP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my hon. friend of Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) for his quite interesting outline of the problem. He will understand however that he has already obtained an answer from the minister, to the effect that the requested docu-

ment contains a legal opinion and knowing his experience and his authority, he surely approves the government for not acceding to his request.
The Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) objected to the motion for the production of copy of a letter which he wrote on October 21, 1974 to the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) in connection with a grant to a women's group in Saskatchewan, because, according to a well established practice, the opinions of legal officers of the Crown on governmental policy matters being included among privileged documents, they have generally not been delivered. I refer him in this connection to page 272 of the 17th edition of May's Parliamentary Practice as well as to page 338 of Bourinot's Parliamentary Procedure.
The guideline governing notices of motions for the production of papers was put forward by the government and printed as an appendix to Hansard of March 15, 1973, on page 2288. The fact that all or part of the documents containing that opinion may have been made available to information media does not constitute a valid reason to break away from traditions preventing the disclosure of such secret documents. If mandatory disclosure applied to such papers, the freedom of expression and the frankness that are essential in the good conduct of public affairs would be seriously jeopardized and the exercise of the responsibility of guiding ministers of the Crown would thus be paralyzed.
On December 10, 1945, a member of Parliament introduced a motion for the production of copies of all orders in council, legal opinions, correspondence and other documents kept by various departments concerning the investigation on a suit for damages caused by an explosion at the marine powder depot in Bedford Basin. The minister, Mr. Mahew, replied that negotiations were under way and that it was impossible to give the hon. member a complete answer. He could give specific information, but it would have required several months to give all data. He then asked that the motion be withdrawn. Mr. St. Laurent, the Minister of Justice, added that his department refused to table texts of legal opinions submitted to other departments. This would be an evident departure from the principle of professional secrecy between a client and his lawyer. If it were the client who had to convey an opinion he had received, things might be different, but he would not like it inferred that when a department seeks the advice of the Department of Justice, the latter may not respect concerning these opinions the principle of professional secrecy which exists in all areas covering the relationship between a client and his lawyer. There were discussions on whether or not the motion should be stricken out. The Speaker stated that, since a motion for papers is not debatable, it was not permissible to rise on a point of order about it.
So that my colleagues may deal for a few minutes with this issue, I shall conclude by saying that I have been very much impressed by the arguments put forward by my hon. colleague about the availability of information to members of Parliament.
In my opinion, the hon. member is right. A member's work should be considered as privileged in a certain way;
February 27, 1975

perhaps he should have access to more information than he has now. On the other hand, if confidentiality and public interest often clash with our work as parliamentarians, it will take a smart one to draw a final line.
Perhaps today's debate will make us more conscious of how important it is to look into the matter more closely and with a great open-mindedness, so that we might consider parliamentarians, whatever their political affiliation, as being people who run a country and thus, need more information.
Mt. Raynald Guay (Parliamentary Secretary to Postmaster General): Mr. Speaker, since I have only a few minutes, I would like to give a brief outline of the situation relating to access to government documents, particularly as far as ordinary members' work is concerned, as mentioned by the previous speaker.
Mr. Speaker, Canada has inherited parliamentary traditions which are cherished and, at the same time, administrative discretion which is one of the greatest barriers between the citizen and the central government and which largely conditions the climate in which the latter carries out its information duties. Canadian scholars are aware of the basic conflict existing between administrative secrecy and the need for information in an active democracy.
At the highest level of our political system, decisions are made in Cabinet, by ministers who swear to keep confidential all issues dealt with, discussed and resolved in Privy Council. The press, the public, the opposition parties and even hon. members often note their powerlessness to get information related to the administration of this country.
In Canada, except for the Official Secrets Act, no regulation prevents or allows access to official documents. A decree is being drafted which will set up the procedures opening access to those documents. On May 1, 1969, the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) announced that our country too was getting prepared to adopt a policy aimed at making it easier for researchers and others to gain access to federal government documents dated before July 1, 1939, and this within the limits of the national interest.
The Prime Minister went on to say that this new policy would show the desire of the government to stimulate the interest and participation of Canadians generally in the affairs of state. It has been said in the House of Commons that this was a very trivial measure, and outside the House, that this measure was not going far enough. The Royal Commission of Inquiry on National Security advocated constantly reminding departments and officials of the advisability of lowering the security on documents. However, they add that in doing so, ministers should be allowed as much discretion as possible. For example, direct access to public papers through government publications has always been freer in Canada and in the United States than in most other western democracies.
In a brief dated June 1967 dealing with the implementation of the information act, the U.S. attorney general stated:
-information distribution must be the general rule and not the exception, that all citizens have equal rights of access, that the burden of
Government Information
justifying the confidential nature of a document is on the government and not the petitioner.
The new legislation sets out for the first time legal procedures enabling a citizen who feels that his rights are encroached upon to lodge a complaint against an agency that refuses without apparent reason to disclose papers. Federal courts have the right to punish directors of official agencies for non-compliance.
As far as public access to government papers is concerned, the French system, for example, seems to be more restrictive than the others was examined, including Canada's. Records are no longer confidential or privileged the very day a minister authorizes the communication of documents pertaining to a specific period. In that respect, there are no automatic provisions in France such as the 30-year rule they have in the United States and Great Britain, and that has been in effect here for a couple of years.
Sweden has recognized for nearly 200 years that all government papers are of public nature unless otherwise restricted by the courts. The Swedish system and its open administration are worthy of admiration but are not necessarily easy to adopt to the Canadian situation. The Swedish form of responsible government is far from similar to ours. It might be difficult because of that to transplant successfully in this country the methods of access to public documents in effect in Sweden.
Coming back to Great Britain, a country that gave birth to our parliamentary system, their tradition of administrative secrecy was challenged by academics and was considered by a committee of inquiry on the public service.
Canada is falling behind other countries, including Great Britain, the United States, and more particularly Sweden, with respect to free access to administrative documents by ordinary citizens, members or parliament or newspapermen. But we know from what happened in the United States that legislating is not a panacea. It is possible to get round the law and twist its purpose. A constant watch has to be kept in order to make sure that access to free information, once enshrined in statutes, is an actual fact.
The consequences of that principle of free access to information are sometimes excessively feared. No one ever talked seriously about lifting all restrictions applying to document consultation. Even in Sweden, there are a number of serious restrictions. The advantage of the Swedish system is that citizens can see a practicial application of their democratic system. Yet, in my opinion, it is logical to think that anyone, a citizen and a taxpayer, may have the right to have access to documents dealing with him in some particular way, without necessarily admitting that he should be allowed unlimited access to information concerning other people. In fact, that might be prejudicial to those people, and I think in that respect we should stick to the principle of a basic prudence. In studying this motion put forward by the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) I have to conclude my remarks considering the principles that have been displayed here, by saying that if we consider what is going on throughout the world with respect to information, and if we look into our parliamentary system, the democratic system which rules our country, we cannot really find in

February 27, 1975
Government Information
any other nation a system which might apply directly to Canada as far as access to administrative documents is concerned.
I therefore had, Mr. Speaker, to thank the hon. member for Fundy-Royal for his remarks which I agree with mostly. However, I cannot say I fully endorse the representations he made this afternoon, and which in fact he had already made several times during other parliaments. They really are very interesting, and I dare hope the government, the departments and the whole cabinet will take good notice of them to help us devise and pass once and for all regulations governing access to so-called social and administrative documents.
I thank the hon. member for his participation. The House may rest assured that if, in the near future, the government is in a position to take a definite stand, I will be most happy about it.
