subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I had ten minutes in which to start my comments on second reading debate of Bill C-46, and at that time I emphasized the importance of public housing if the most urgent needs of Canadians for housing were to be met.
I also spoke of the important role to be played by co-operative and non-profit housing as the third force in the housing field, and I quoted some words of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford), who at the time was the minister of state for urban affairs, on the subject of co-operative housing and non-profit corporations in the field of housing. I noted that he mentioned the fact that neighbourhood groups in these organizations have a vital role to play. I also mentioned that in my constituency Forward Nine Community Development Co-operative set up a housing co-operative, which now has 75 units, which they have rehabilitated and rented at moderate and low rentals. The project, I pointed out, was well managed, highly successful, and provided a model which others could copy.
I asked what the government had done. Last year parliament passed an act to amend the National Housing Act,
National Housing Act
and by section 18 of that act it amended section 44 of the previous NHA to provide in subsection 1(b) that CMHC might enter into agreement with non-profit corporations and co-operatives to make contributions for the purpose of assisting to provide housing accommodation to individuals, or families with low income, at rentals that were less than those required to meet the cost of amortizing and operating the public housing project.
It seems to me that with the passage of that act a little more than a year ago there was a clear direction by parliament to the government to proceed in the field of assisting co-operative housing, nor was the legislation in any sense restrictive as to the nature or manner of assistance. However, its implementation clearly requires the allocation of adequate funds. So far as I can make out, no such funds have in fact been allocated under section 44(1) (b). To be fair I must say that I have corresponded with the minister on this subject, and one of his assistants assured me on the telephone that when other difficulties- which I will come to in a moment-were solved, such funds would be provided. I would like, at some stage during the discussion of this bill, to hear more from the minister on this point.
Another problem which has arisen in connection with co-operative housing concerns the contribution of the federal government in respect to rental supplements. I have already referred to a seminar which took place in Toronto on March 25, to which were invited the representatives of non-profit and co-operative housing. I mentioned that the former minister was present there and gave an enthusiastic endorsement to the section dealing with co-operative and non profit housing, which he called the third sector.
The then Ontario minister of housing, Mr. Sidney Han-dleman, spoke of the close consultation between the two senior levels of government in respect to this third sector. He went on to describe the necessity for a rent supplement, and the federal minister sitting there expressed no dissent, at least judging from what he said. Later a committee was formed to discuss the need for an adjustment of the supplemental program and to work out its details. On this committee were a large number of community developers representing projects in different parts of Ontario, a municipal liaison committee, and representatives from the Ontario regional office of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
This committee made a report on May 10 of last year setting out a number of guidelines in regard to these rental supplements, and further progress was made. One agreement was reached involving a modification of the rule that no more than 25 per cent of the non-profit project would be supplemented and would be subject to supplemental assistance. The CMHC representatives were there, and apparently went along with that agreement.
In December the plans of the Forward Nine Co-operative, and no doubt, of many other co-operatives, to take advantage of the rent supplement plan, were advanced when their project was approved by a provincial order in council. There was a provincial order in council approving the projects involving rent supplements, after several months of discussion. But difficulties intervened. Where

National Housing Act
did the difficulties come from? They came from the representatives of the federal government.
People were told that the federal government regulations were not in place. This was more than a year and a half since legislation had been passed providing for assistance to co-operatives, but their regulations were not yet in place at the beginning of this year, and it was stated that under the federal regulations senior citizens were to be excluded from rent supplemented accommodation. This was put forward on the grounds that there were other forms of legislation dealing with senior citizens.
If it is true that this objection was made, to my mind it is utterly unreasonable. Everyone knows that the integration of senior citizens with the rest of the community is highly desirable, and in a co-operative low rental project this was obviously a sound and a necessary thing.
So desperate was the situation that the Forward Nine Co-operative sent a telegram to the minister. I had it here, but I don't know where it is at the moment. I will paraphrase it from memory. In that telegram the co-operative said that their whole co-operative project was threatened with disaster unless these matters could be cleared up quickly. No doubt while I am quoting this one project in my own constituency, there are many more of these projects which are in exactly the same position.
I wrote to the minister on January 16 telling him my views on what I called a crisis for co-operative housing in Canada. He has not yet had time to respond to my letter, but one of his assistants was good enough to phone me and tell me that considerable progress had been made and that settlement of outstanding problems in regard to the regulations and the methods of operation of the rental supplement in co-operative housing was expected shortly.
I do not know whether as yet the regulations are finally in place after these months of delay. I do not know whether the funds have been made available, or when they will be made available. I acknowledge that this so-called third sector, of which the minister's predecessor spoke with such enthusiasm, is only beginning to emerge, but I plead with the minister-I notice he does not have the time to listen to me now, but perhaps he will read what I have to say; or perhaps his attitude reveals the degree of his interest in co-operative housing-that if any real meaning is to be given to the words of his predecessor and to the provisions of parliament in respect to co-operative housing, then we must have promptly the necessary regulations, and the necessary funds made available.
I say it would be tragic if the detailed plans made by the co-operatives themselves in agreement with the Ontario government-and apparently acquiesced in by the representatives of CMHC-should be allowed to fail. I ask the minister to make it clear that he adopts the same enthusiastic attitude as his predecessor to the role of the third sector, namely, co-operative and non-profit housing. I want to make sure that he tells us that he agrees with the words of his predecessor about the vital importance of this particular sector of housing.
I do not believe that co-operative housing is the total solution to this problem, but it has an important contribution to make. I think it would be a betrayal of the whole co-operative movement, of co-operative principles, of the

plans which have been made and, indeed, of what parliament has authorized, if we are to have further delays and inadequacy of response to this need.
I understand that the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent), the parliamentary leader of my party, is going to speak in this debate on the reason for our opposition to this bill. I will not attempt to go over that ground, but I do want to put my views in a nutshell.
The direction of the bill is once again the wrong direction. The emphasis is on assistance to financial institutions. The beneficiaries are once again those who need it least. We reject the philosophy that housing aid should be denied to those in most urgent need and provided for those who need it least. We must oppose this legislation which exemplifies the application of that philosophy which we reject.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS TO AMOUNT OF INSURED LOANS, TO INCREASE CAPITAL OF CORPORATIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in this House to express my concern regarding this totally inadequate amendment of the National Housing Act. My hon. colleagues have spoken well and criticized the amendments, and they have proposed substantial improvements such as legislation to allow taxes and mortgage interest payments to be deducted from federal income tax, which is of more help for rural homeowners who, under the present system, cannot get mortgages from CMHC unless they are hooked up to municipal sewers. I wonder what is wrong with a good septic tank? If the land has the capacity, this is an adequate means of disposing of sewage.
The other ideas brought forward, the extension of the $500 grant to first time buyers of existing homes, the extension of the Veterans' Land Act past March 31, 1975, the increased availability of mortgage money at reduced interest rates, are commendable. Tonight my concern, however, is the apparent and even reasonable suspicion and fear that Canadians feel when government sponsored housing projects are proposed. Too often in the history of public housing, here and in other countries, government sponsored and developed housing units stand as monumental examples of high density, low income, low cost, substandard ghetto-type housing which creates a host of social and economic evils.
We should not be surprised at the reaction of local politicians and citizens as the senior governments come bearing these questionable gifts. The only surprise we should feel is that people did not realize much sooner the type of development that was proposed. Some of the biggest housing disasters in the world have occurred as a result of the actions of well-intentioned governments. There are many slums as a result of this type of thing.
Municipalities have not just occasionally suffered as a result of the actions of developers but have suffered even more through governments promoting this high density, low quality concept as a pragmatic and expedient political answer to housing demand and need. Now that the community has experienced some of the side effects of creating and repeating this destruction of liveability, not only are municipal governments resisting development but so are the residents who naturally, and rightly so, want to
February 27, 1975

protect their life style and the environment. This suspicion is accompanied by delays and escalations in construction costs. These will continue until the government shows innovative leadership in reaching beyond the mere creation of a housing unit and begins to concentrate on placing and integrating homes within highly desirable communities and environments.
The tools and the opportunities are available in this country now, Mr. Speaker, and I am optimistic that the minister and his administration have the expertise to do the job. If they have the will and the energy, they can lead the way in innovative housing for Canada and the world.
I hope the government will never be so total that it has the capacity to provide all the housing units required by Canadians. I would say, however, that it has an obligation, through example, to show the way in innovative horsing development, and I would say that the opportunity is available here and now.
I call tonight for a concerted and co-ordinated effort by all levels of government to demonstrate leadership in the area of housing through the construction of a model community as a demonstration project in conjunction with the upcoming United Nations Conference on Human Settlements-Habitat-to be held in Vancouver in 1976.
What I propose is the construction of a model community which would incorporate the best ideas and efforts of all levels of government in co-operation with experts in the fields of urban planning, transportation, sanitation, construction, the environment and finance. Input would also be sought from sociologists, psychologists, recreational experts, consumers' groups, and tenants' associations. Hopefully, the result would be a community concept which stresses low density and an interrelationship of man and his environment to their maximum mutual benefit.
The people in my constituency were recently alarmed by a government proposal to develop a 5,000 acre city at Burke Mountain, adjacent to the greater Vancouver area. Through past experience with government proposals they feel they have good cause to fear that their lifestyle will be destroyed and replaced by high density, low cost, low income housing, with all its social and economic disruption. This need not be the way, however. The Burke Mountain area qualifies in every respect for a world model demonstration project. Canada shows leadership in many fields. I think we can be justly proud of the World's Fair in Montreal, and we are again showing leadership in promoting the Olympic Games in Montreal. But I think Canada can do more than that. We can show leadership in housing as well.
A conference has been arranged to be held in Vancouver to talk about human settlement. I think it is important that this should not just produce another pile of paper to be recycled. We should be taking advantage of the expertise that will be coming from all over the world. We should have a model ready to be presented to the conference, and we should welcome the input from people from older civilizations. They could travel out to see this beautiful site. Burke Mountain is a low level mountain, with forests, ravines and rivers. It has a tremendous potential for development, but of course many people would prefer that it remain in its present condition on the periphery of de-
National Housing Act
velopment of one of Canada's largest cities. But it is inevitable that the area will be developed, and it has already been marked for this by the municipal and provincial governments.
Instead of creating another housing project with more dwelling units, I think we should take this opportunity to create something in tune with the environment, and develop this project as a world model. There will be other models at the conference, of subdivisions and so on, but I am talking about a major world innovative project based on the best planning available in Canada, and supplemented by the expertise available at the world conference.
I am pleased that the response to this project has been positive, and I commend the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) and the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Sauve) for showing interest. Mayor Tonn of Coquitlam and the council are most enthusiastic as well. I have also spoken with the premier of British Columbia and his minister of housing, who have both expressed interest.
I am pleased to announce tonight that I have arranged a meeting for March 5 to be chaired by Dr. Walter Hardwick of the University of British Columbia, to consider this proposal further. I should thank the ministers involved for making the expertise of their staffs available to us, and I should thank as well members on all sides of the House who will, I hope, be represented at this meeting. I think it is important to note that the province of British Columbia, the regional districts and the municipalities are coordinating their efforts in a non-political, non-partisan way in order to try to do something about a major problem in this country.
I call on the minister to examine the ideas I have put forward. Let him apply money and expertise to the solution of our housing problems. Let him confer with the head of Central Mortgage and Housing. A good beginning has been made in Ottawa with a model development. Similar developments ought to be encouraged. I hope the minister will encourage other similar programs and make them realities, so that he, as the housing minister for all Canada, will lead the way in bringing about solutions.

Mr. Speaker, in talking on this bill on behalf of my party let me state precisely how we look on housing.
We begin by assuming that housing is not a commodity, not a chattel, not a service like any other in society. It should not be a resource which we can or cannot buy, depending on income. We do not liken it, for instance, to something like colour television, which one can or cannot afford, depending on income, or to an expensive automobile, which one can or cannot buy, again depending on income. We do not think housing can be regarded as a commodity of that kind.
We believe that housing, like medical services and like education, at least up to university level, should be available as a basic social right. Housing is a right to which every Canadian family is entitled by virtue of being part of our society. We test housing legislation by asking how it conforms to this general principle. We ask does the legislation recognize that housing is a social right, that

February 27, 1975
National Housing Act
houses are not a commodity like any other in society? Second, if the legislation recognizes housing as a right, does it do something to fulfil that right? If the legislation meets either test, particularly if it meets our first point, we supported it, even though it may not go far enough in providing all the necessary details. Certainly the first test is crucial. The measure before the House completely fails to meet that test. There could not be a more clear revelation of Liberal philosophy on housing, a philosophy which has certainly continued since 1968 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office.
Of the many ministers and departments which have been given responsibility for housing, not one has brought forward legislation clearly embodying the notion that housing is a social right. Actually the legislation which has come forward has suggested just the opposite, namely, that the market will ultimately determine whether a Canadian family will obtain a house. Any mechanisms introduced by the government for providing housing have been aimed at the banks, trust companies and other financial institutions. The aim of the government has always been to give incentives to these basically market-oriented institutions to provide services.
It is morally absurd and economically fallacious to pretend that our housing needs can be, or ought to be met by policies of this kind. Legislation of this kind is as outdated as legislation would be which tried to reverse the principle of medicare. But that is precisely what this government continues to do; I shall show later exactly how it does so.
First let me say something about the real housing needs of Canadians. What is the situation? The minister himself, according to an interview reported in the Ottawa Citizen last October, acknowledged that Canada still needs to establish a minimum of 800,000 new housing units, which includes new housing as well as rehabilitated units. Altogether we need a minimum of 800,000 newly established housing units for the people of Canada. That figure was mentioned by the minister; he was not far wrong, and I give him credit for acknowledging the need. On the other hand the Canadian Council on Social Development says that we need one million units if we are to meet the housing needs of Canadians.
What is the human meaning of the figures mentioned by the minister and by the Canadian Council on Social Development? They mean that four million Canadians are inadequately housed. That is what the figures mean in human terms. They mean, as the minister knows very well, that more than 50 per cent of our native people are grotesquely under-housed. They mean that people in the Maritimes are inadequately housed to a disproportionate extent, and that people in our large cities, in Toronto, Vancouver and Montreal in particular, are inadequately housed. They mean that four million Canadians, men, women and children of every racial origin in our society, are inadequately housed. Surely in a society enjoying one of the highest per capita incomes in the world in 1975, this situation is unjustified. There is no excuse for it, considering our present economic potential. I am not talking about Utopia. I am talking about the state of our economy in 1975. The fact that four million Canadians are inadequately housed should make us, as legislators, ashamed.

What about housing starts? The minister himself acknowledged the need. But what has been the record of the government and of the minister? In 1974 we saw 222,000 housing units constructed. That figure does not represent an increase. It is the lowest number of new units built since 1970; it is the lowest number built in four years. Instead of increasing, our housing starts are declining. The minister expressed the hope that in 1975, 210,000 units will be built. That is a lower figure than the one applying to 1974. He is not increasing the number of units which are to be built each year. He acknowledges as a target a lower figure, a lower number of units than was built last year.
We discovered, when we saw the figures for January, that if the present rate of construction is projected forward for the rest of the year, instead of even 210,000 units being built to meet the minister's target, only 176,000 will be built.

If we could have order, Mr. Speaker, it would be nice to hear some substance instead of wind from the Conservative party. I would be interested in getting a serious question from them at any time.
If you take the rate of inflation in general and the rate of inflation in housing in particular, there is in fact a reduction in real dollars in the government's housing budget for 1975. The minister must admit that. I look forward to his comments on that later in the debate.
One provincial minister of housing estimated that, far from being an increase, there has been a 20 per cent reduction in real dollars allocated for housing. I do not necessarily say it is 20 per cent. However, I do say there is no increase in the amount of money to be spent on housing by the government. Surely that is totally unacceptable.
Let me say something about mortgage rates. In 1974 mortgage rates went as high as 13 per cent. They recently came down a bit, and are now about 11 per cent. Second mortgages are still going at between 14 and 16 per cent. What does this mean in basic human terms?
On the average mortgage a family has to pay approximately $250 a month just for the interest rates. They are paying some bank or other financial institution $250 a month. How many people in Canada can afford that? The question is rhetorical. The minister knows that in terms of income, it excludes about 80 per cent of the families in Canada. They simply cannot afford to pay that. Surely it is an unacceptable situation. If we regarded housing like we regard medicare, we would make a change in our financial administration so that families do not have to get into that kind of bind, and the majority of families would be able to buy houses.
What about housing costs? In 1974 the average price of a home in Canada was $42,000. From west to east the provincial averages are as follows: British Columbia, $43,200; Alberta, $37,200; Saskatchewan, $24,000; Manitoba, the data is not yet available; Ontario, $46,900; Quebec, $32,900, and the Atlantic provinces, $30,500. I again ask rhetorically,
National Housing Act
how many Canadians can afford homes in that price range? The answer, of course, is very few.
What is the general conclusion? After considering the supply of housing the government hopes to bring on the market, the mortgage situation, prices for 1974, and what they are likely to be in 1975, the conclusion is inevitable. The poor in our society, that 20 per cent of Canadians who live below the poverty level, are right out of the picture in terms of being able to afford housing in this country. There is no way they fit into the market. That is the first point.
The second question is where does the average family of the lumberman on the west coast, the packinghouse worker in Toronto and the steadily employed person in Halifax, find itself in terms of being able to purchase a house? I am talking about the regularly employed family which is not afflicted by unemployment or living on an inordinately low income. The fact is that it too is excluded from the housing market.
Young families simply cannot afford to buy houses in most places in Canada, even though their incomes are quite reasonable in terms of existence in society in a general way. In short, whether we consider the poor or the average family, housing is by no means a social right. It is still very much a commodity in the market place, to be bought or not bought by those with a substantial amount of income at their disposal. Housing is far from being a social right. It is still the privilege of the affluent in society. It is out of reach for the vast majority of Canadians, but so far the government has not done anything about it.
I have referred to the past and current market situation. Now, I ask what about the minister's bill? It deals with four areas. First, there is AHOP, the Assisted Home Ownership Program, that marvellous election promise of the Liberals. This legislation provides a subsidy of up to $600. However, who gets that money? It will not directly benefit the low or average income earners. The Liberal party, true to its historic traditions, has decided to subsidize the banks. It is a continuation of the corporate rip-off.
The typical solution of the Liberal party is to help the poor by giving money to the rich and hoping it will trickle down. I see the minister shaking his head, the implication being that this is not a subsidy to the banks. I will point out how I think it is a subsidy, and the minister can correct me.
Let me use the example of a mortgage rate of 10 3A per cent. A family may qualify for the AHOP loan and receive the maximum $600. What procedures are followed? This may bring down the mortgage rate that family has to pay by two percentage points, to 894 per cent. Does this mean the bank gets only 8 3A per cent? Of course not. The bank will still get 10 3A per cent because the great generosity of the Liberal party is going to provide that $600 to the family on condition it is passed on immediately to the banks.
All this program does is provide money to the banks from the pockets of the taxpayers of Canada, and channel it through the hands of the people who need housing. It does nothing at all to force the banks to bring down

February 27, 1975
National Housing Act
interest rates. It does everything to increase their profit margin.
The program is harmful, too, inasmuch as it takes the pressure off the banks to bring down mortgage rates. To put it in blunt terms, why the hell should they? Why should they bring down mortgage rates if the government is going to subsidize them at present levels? So they keep them high, and hope the government will continue to pay people money to pass on to them. Apart from that, it is a waste of money. It is estimated that for 1975 the cost of this marvelous, new, progressive legislation will be about $35 million. I say it is a gift to the banks.
If the government wanted to make a sensible amendment to the AHOP program it could borrow money at 9 per cent. I should like to get the minister's attention so that he could reply to this point.

If it really wishes to benefit the people instead of the banks why does not the federal government borrow money at 9 per cent, which is the current rate it pays for funds, then apply the subsidy itself and put the money out at 7 per cent, instead of getting it through the banks and subsidizing the high mortgage rates? The government can get money at 9 per cent. Why should it subsidize the banks at 10 3A per cent? The method now proposed is totally unjustified, even accepting the basic assumptions of the Liberal party.
Next, the bill provides financial incentives for private developers, encouraging them to build more rental accommodation. Once again this program is a direct subsidy to the developers so that they will build more houses. It is a giveway to the developers.
The third aspect of the bill is that dealing with nonprofit housing corporations. I must say that when I read this part I thought there had been a terrible mistake in the legislation. I reached that conclusion because the bill seemed to make sense. How, I asked myself, could the Liberals be proposing to acquire land for non-profit housing? I thought there had been a grotesque error somewhere-that somebody on the Treasury Board or in the department had made a mistake. However, reading on, I found my prejudices about the Liberal party were confirmed.
I discovered that though they had decided to acquire land for private housing they intended to remove the 10 per cent capital grant which was formerly available. In effect, they were saying to the poor people right across the country, "We shall buy this land for you, so go ahead and build your housing units; at the same time we are taking away the 10 per cent capital grant we formerly provided." That is a typical piece of shifty work by the Liberal party. They give with one hand and take away with the other to make sure there is not redistribution of wealth in the country-that would fly in the face of everything that party stands for, Mr. Speaker.

Next, the government is to provide assistance in connection with sewage systems to municipalities. Here I am glad to say the Liberals have done something which in principle one cannot object to, and the amendments in this area make sense. One could quibble about detail, but I will rest there. I think it makes sense. Even though it is brought in by the minister responsible for housing I still think it is good, and he must be given credit.
To sum up, three of the four aspects of this housing legislation are totally contradictory to the principle that housing should be a social right.
What is an alternative approach, in 1975, which recognizes that we need a million new units and acknowledges at the same time that behind the statistics are four million Canadian lives? What if we took housing seriously as a social objective, recognizing that housing is a social right, and that unemployment is running at 7 or 8 per cent? First, instead of $1.2 billion for housing the budget should be at least twice that amount for 1975. This would also mean a serious commitment to creating thousands of jobs in a year which will likely be the worst in terms of numbers unemployed than any year since the depression. So, in terms of facing up to a social responsibility it makes sense, and in terms of creating the number of housing units we need it makes sense. That is the first step we should take.
Second, instead of relying on the private sector, instead of providing financial incentives and all kinds of rip-off opportunities, the money should be channelled through public hands and kept entirely in public hands until it gets to the people who really need housing. How could that principle be implemented?
Let me deal first with land assembly, which represents a major cost of housing. The federal government should duplicate on a national basis what the Manitoba government has done.
The Manitoba government in Winnipeg-I see the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) listening to my remarks and perhaps he will interject on this point- through the means of public land assembly found it could buy land, provide the servicing required in the form of sewers, water and so on, and sell lots for $7,000 a unit. That is exactly half the price that the commercial market has established in the city of Winnipeg today. The kind of financial incentive, the free market wheeling and dealing that is supported by the Liberals and Conservatives sees lots selling in the same city of Winnipeg for $14,000, twice the price of land assembled publicly by the government of Manitoba.
That demonstrates that a government that wants to regard housing as a social right, and which uses governmental authority in the interest of the people, can bring down land costs by 50 per cent. I should like to see this kind of program duplicated across the country on a national basis, and a government committed to this would put up the funds that would enable such a program to be implemented.
The second point I want to make is connected with mortgages. Instead of providing charity to the banks and using millions of dollars of taxpayers' money under AHOP
February 27, 1975

to subsidize the banks, as the minister is in this crass legislation, what the government should do is to amend all legislation pertaining to the Bank of Canada and financial institutions so as to make it mandatory that banks place a certain percentage of their investments in mortgages at 6 per cent.
I see the minister shaking his head in bewilderment, and I do not doubt it, because what is involved in this suggestion is the taking on of the banks in our society. It is exactly analogous to what the government of Saskatchewan did a few years ago when it brought in medicare. The NDP government said that medical care was a social right. Every other reactionary force in society, including the Liberal party of Saskatchewan and the Tories, said no, we could not do that. They said we could not challenge the medical profession in that kind of way. But we did in Saskatchewan, and within a few years all other parties across Canada suddenly discovered that you could take on the medical profession. They suddenly discovered that the majority of Canadians liked medicare.
I say that the majority of Canadians would like more money at 6 per cent, but the only way to give it to them is to say to the banks that on a certain part of their investments, they are not going to make a profit. They can make a profit on colour television sets, electric tooth brushes and other gadgets, on the financing of shopping centres and so on; but on any money that they put up for housing for the people of Canada they will not make a profit. Over all in their operations they would still be profitable. A 6 per cent mortgage policy could be implemented on that kind of basis, and on no other. However, I do not expect the Liberal party, which has never been known as a party willing to take on the banks, to understate the position a wee bit, will move in that direction. But if it wanted to it could, and it should.
Finally, the new emphasis on housing policy for low income people in particular should be placed upon co-operative housing. In 1973 the budget for co-op housing was $2 million. It has now been raised to a paltry $4.5 million. If the government wants to make it possible for poor Canadians to get housing, then this is the sector into which it should move. Yet it has allocated a paltry $4.5 million. If the government wanted to express a genuine concern on the part of this parliament for the real housing needs of the people, it should expand this sector of its housing budget beyond what it is at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to have the opportunity of making a few comments on a bill which strikes me as very important for all Canadians, and which, in addition, represents an element of prime importance in our economy.
I am sure the government recognizes the urgency of intervening quickly in this problem of prime importance to all Canadians, but again, I feel the government proves incapable of implementing the required measures.
I should like to point out to the House, Mr. Speaker, that though the bill now being studied is not bad in itself, it does not meet the real needs of Canadians where housing and urbanism are concerned. We are at grips with what seems to me to be a fundamental economic problem in Canada, which needs to be resolved as quickly as possible. As I said a moment ago, this bill falls far short of suggesting the solutions needed to the housing problem in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, a housing policy for Canada has been for many years part of the Social Credit Party platform. Everybody knows that this is a serious problem which affects all Canadians, and this is one of the reasons why the Social Credit Party of Canada strongly supports the development of a housing policy.
I suggest that, although it may be sound theoretically, the housing policy which is set forth in this bill would not work. The grants will benefit people with above average income, while small earners will not be eligible. It is high time, Madam Speaker, for the government to become aware of this problem. The government should unquestionably increase the grants to small earners, thereby giving them once and for all access to single dwelling housing. I feel that the changes to the bill are very important and acceptable as a whole, but that this bill is still incomplete, imperfect and, as such, fully out of touch with the needs of the underprivileged.
I am delighted to see that the bill provides increased assistance to non-profit making housing projects and to housing co-operatives as well as federal programs of land rentals for non-profit making and co-operative housing. Moreover, I think that the latter will enable the corporation to purchase and improve lots and rent them at a very low price to non-profit making corporations. Another amendment which seems to be important but only for some people is the aid granted by the government to facilitate the purchase of a house. On the other hand, I consider that the low amount of $500 granted for that purpose will be insufficient for individuals with low incomes.
Since housing is essential for all, that it is a consumer's item which is costly, it is undeniable that we must deal with the matter in order to help the underprivileged as soon as possible.

National Housing Act
I think it would also be advisable for the government to provide and build homes for senior citizens, because most projects are on a cost-share basis and unfortunately, funds are often earmarked for this or that project and the province of Quebec, particularly, uses them according to its own priorities. We all know that there is a lot of confusion and unrest in Quebec now. I think that the federal government would be well advised to assume its responsibilities and build homes for senior citizens and for people with low income. It should build moderately priced housing, as is more and more the case now.
As recent statistics show, in many families, 30 per cent of the budget goes to housing. This means that the cost of housing represents about a third of the consumer price index. The most affected by this remain citizens with a low income.
Madam Speaker, housing is essential to all Canadians. He must fight against the hardship of winter and have a home where he can fill his needs.
Today, it is almost impossible to buy a house, considering loans are for a 40-year period, and this only tends to sink people into debt for 40 years. We all know that under current standards houses have a guaranteed life span of 20 years. But contrary to logic loans are made for a 40-year term. After 20 years, the house is finished and the sad owner is left with another 20 years of payments. What for? Absolutely nothing. The house is uncomfortable, and he might as well live out in the open.
As I indicated, it is almost impossible to own a house today, considering loans are granted for a 40-year period. This is discouraging for people. I feel someone wishing to build a house of any type should be able to repay in ten years. But it is the opposite way. A great many people own houses guaranteed for 25, and even 40 years, still carrying mortgages higher than their value, to the point that owners cannot even repay, and let them go.
Madam Speaker, I would like to discuss some ways of giving each Canadian the opportunity of getting decent housing on normal terms.
As a first solution, interest rates should be brought down, since they are very high, and money should be made more readily available to every citizen, because each one of necessity must find shelter.
One of the points the government has finally understood is the lowering of the sale tax on building materials from 12 to 5 per cent. That reduction is most likely to end in a smaller increase in the cost of a house, rather than in an immediate lowering. Moreover, Madam Speaker, are we Social Crediters not the ones who have been calling for that for many years? Yes, Madam Speaker. This example has been followed by builders and real estate agents as well as by consumers. One thing is sure: that reduction does not immediately really influence the price of a singlefamily house, and the next increase will certainly be countered or less steep.
Once again, we urge the government to encourage Canadians to build single-family houses by guaranteeing them long-term loans at an administrative rate. Furthermore, we would like single-family house owners to benefit as well from a tax reduction equivalent to the interests

they pay on mortgages and the amount of their school and municipal taxes.

subtopic: BROADCASTING-CODE GOVERNING STANDARDS OF TELEVISION PROGRAMS

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: BROADCASTING-CODE GOVERNING STANDARDS OF TELEVISION PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on February 13, as recorded at page 3185 of Hansard, I directed a question to the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier) regarding the need for regulations putting into place guidelines to govern sex and violence on Canadian television. My question was prompted by a number of questions raised in the House by a number of concerned members of parliament over the growing tendency by Canadian television, and especially CBC, to depict violence on programs and to portray explicit sex scenes and offensive language.
Like most decent people in this country, and especially parents in this country, I am becoming fed up, as, I am sure, many hon. members are, with this tendency. I can say that I am growing extremely impatient with the failure of the statutory authority, in this case the CRTC, to enforce regulations in accordance with the mandate they have under the Broadcasting Act that would specifically prohibit broadcasters, especially CBC, from offending the morals and mores of the vast majority of people in this country. Hardly a week goes by in which there is not such an offending program that contains offensive language, explicit sex scenes, and violence bordering on sadism.
I will be the first to admit that there is little or no evidence to indicate that explicit sex on television is harmful to young minds, but there are few who would disagree that sex on television offends our Judaeo-Chris-tian moral standards, whether it is the Friday night blue movies in Toronto or what passes off as Canadian content on CBC television. I doubt very much if there is a member of this House who has not received a letter from an irate constituent who was shocked by what he had seen on Canadian television, and especially in recent years on the CBC.
But there is a real case to be made about the harmful effects of violence on television. Violent crime is on the increase in Canada as well as in the United States. The Surgeon General of the United States, when he appeared before a U.S. senate subcommittee a few months ago, reported on a study that had been made by a scientific
Adjournment Debate
committee covering a period of two years. This was his blunt conclusion:
"The overwhelming consensus and the unanimous Scientific Advisory Committee's report indicate that televised violence, indeed, does have an adverse effect on certain members of our society ... It is clear to me that the casual relationship between televised violence and anti-social behaviour is sufficient to warrant appropriate and immediate remedial action ...
A research scientist at Stanford University said that there is exposure to violence on television and that:
... aggressive behaviour on a one-time basis can be repeated in free play by as high as 88 per cent of the young children seeing it on TV.
Even in our own country there is concern. A few weeks ago the Solicitor General for Canada (Mr. Allmand), in a speech in Toronto said, and I quote from a press report:
... that his department is studying television violence and may limit programs containing violence if it concludes they encourage aggressive behaviour.
I quote again from another Canadian source, and this is a recent press report:
Chief Justice George Gale of Ontario's Court of Appeal has urged entertainment industries purge themselves of excessive violence as part of an attack on urban crime.
He went on to say:
... "it's little wonder children eventually go out and try to practice what they have seen.''
In the very few minutes at my disposal on this adjournment debate obviously I cannot go into the arguments in any substantive way. I believe that the evidence is in, and it warrants action on the part of the government through its agency in this regard, the Canadian Radio Television Commission. I might say that the counterpart of the CRTC in the United States, the FCC, recently asked the United States congress to enact legislation to sharpen up the definition of obscenity so that that commission can put into place regulations which would govern the growing tendency on the part of United States broadcasters to use programs which exploit sex and violence. I believe that there should have been some action on the part of the CRTC in Canada.
There should be regulations, and the least the government should do is immediately embark on a program of public hearings which would have, as the end result, the promulgation of guidelines which would govern the use of sex, violence and offensive language on television, and which would have the effect of satisfying what I believe to be the very great concern of a majority of people in this country.

subtopic: BROADCASTING-CODE GOVERNING STANDARDS OF TELEVISION PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the government does not intend to legislate on the matter of forbidding televised violence, nor to impose in the near future a code of ethics in that respect. As for obscenity, it is already dealt with in our legislation. However, considering the importance of that matter and the interest it has aroused, the CBC has informed me that they are looking into the possibility of having a special public hearing, as the hon. member just suggested on that matter of televised violence.

Adjournment Debate
I also got the following representations from the CBC: the matter of a relationship between televised violence and violence as it has been witnessed in human behaviour has been discussed and studied for at least 15 years. The most significant contribution in that respect was made by the United States Surgeon-General's Scientific Advisory Committee on Television and Social Behaviour. That five volume report encompasses more than 50 different studies. Broadly speaking, its conclusions are that televised violence may cause some children to have anti-social behaviour under particular circumstances. The report states for instance that the effects of repeated televised violence may appear on a long term basis or indirectly. However, there is a tendency among a minor group of people to argue that televised violence would attenuate instead of stimulate aggressive impulses, but here again depending on environment and conditions.
No such extensive survey has been undertaken in Canada. However, it has been shown that Canadian television programs display a lesser amount of violence than American made programs. The Canadian Radio-Television Commission recently carried out a detailed analysis of the contents of 53 television programs broadcasted by Canadian television stations in a major Canadian city to determine the proportion of violence in Canadian made programs as compared with American programs. All the programs analysed were aired at times when the greatest number of children are known to be listening. The analysis dealt with 28 entertainment programs made in Canada and 25 in the United States. According to the standards of reference, the analysis showed that out of a total 103 scenes of violence, 95.1 per cent happened in the 25 American made programs, and 4.9 per cent only in the Canadian made programs.
The matter of violence on television is therefore linked with a problem which faces all countries of our western hemisphere since all of them, at least occasionally, buy American series.
Consequently, two conditions will probably become indispensable, over the long term, to remedy the proliferation of scenes of violence, namely: a significant increase in the quantity and quality of Canadian production; and, a change in the influence of marketing strategies on production, the choice and scheduling of programs.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR INCREASED FUNDS FOR DEPARTMENT
AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR INCREASED FUNDS FOR DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, quite recently, I have on a few occasions drawn the attention of the House to the serious problems which are creating upheavals on every hand in our Canadian agriculture. Since the situation seems to be deteriorating almost constantly, I return to the charge once again today with criticism that is meant to be constructive.
Energetic steps must be taken immediately in agriculture. The situation has now really become alarming for our farmers. In 1974, we witnessed a swift increase, without parallel, in the cost of production, namely an increase of 23 per cent. On the other hand, the increase in income amounted to only 17 per cent. To that, for farmers as well as others, a 12 per cent rate of inflation must be added. So

this means that especially in Quebec, despite the few millions of dollars injected by the government of Quebec, agriculture stood in a very precarious situation at the end of the year.
On the one hand, in the budget speech of this year, there was no special provision to support agriculture, which is already depressed, as I clearly indicated at that time in the House. On the other hand, since the beginning of this year, the cost of inputs has been rising steadily.
Besides, the conference on Canadian agricultural outlook for 1975, held in Ottawa last January, indicated that feeds, fertilizers, chemicals, energy, fuel, binder twine, agricultural machinery, electricity and some other items will contribute to raise production costs this year. Furthermore, the economist of Agriculture Canada, Mr. C. R. Phillips, has emphasized that we have every reason to believe that inflation will play the same part in 1975 as it did last year.
This means that the government must act as soon as possible, if we want to avoid an irreparable disaster in agriculture. According to a Department of Agriculture press release on the outlook for 1975, the gross agricultural income will increase by 4 p. 100 in 1975, but the net agricultural income could fall by 12 per cent, mainly because of the increasing cost of production factors.
Madam Speaker, this only means that unfortunately we shall soon be witnessing many bankruptcies and a massive exodus of farmers going to welfare offices, as the list of forthcoming auctions already shows, even in winter. If I must be accused because of my speech, I would rather be accused of saying the truth than hiding it. In any event, nobody could stop things from being what they are.
Besides, Madam Speaker, I would like to give two or three examples showing that agricultural producers will go belly up if the government does not act. First, I must say that most farmers in Quebec now have to pay $100 or more a hundredweight for the hay which they will need until the end of winter. It is a real disaster when you think that it used to cost $30 or $35 a hundredweight.
On the other hand, I have been informed recently that binder twine for hay is selling at $33 a two-roll package. After all, it is not gold twine to reach such an incredible price. Two years ago, the package was selling for about $6.
And what about feeds whose prices keep increasing steadily? In that respect I want to point out that the government must set profiteers straight as soon as possible, even if they are farmers in certain cases. The balance of the whole Canadian agriculture depends on it. I must point out here that I do not want to be the only defender of Quebec farmers but I must expose injustice where I see it. That is why the federal department of Agriculture must intervene vigourously. I quote from an editorial by Francois Dagenais in the newspaper La Terre de Chez Nous of January 22, 1975:
Western Canada is certainly the primary cause of the increase of input costs. Feeds prices spiralled in 1974. Indeed, since the majority of grains come from the West, producers in those provinces experienced revenue increases of around 36 per cent in 1974. Quebec producers contributed in part to that balance which is more than positive.
Madam Speaker, how can the federal department of Agriculture allow such a disparity? I agree that farmers should make profits but not to the extent of some living at

the expense of the others, and with impunity. I am not afraid to say that in the area of agriculture, we are close to an emergency. If we refuse to admit it today, the events in coming months will undoubtedly bring it home to us.
That is why the government must act as soon as possible and require the co-operation of our western grain producers so that grain prices will be acceptable to eastern producers. We can only support our agriculture if everybody co-operates.
There are other solutions on the very short term. I point them out to the minister because I want my criticism to be positive. If, for example, the Department of Transport must greatly reduce freight rates to move grain from the West to the East, let it do so. Emergency measures are needed to deal with an emergency.
Furthermore, Madam Speaker, the government must really expose some large businesses who run monopolies, build up inventories to boast prices, and take undue advantage of the difficult situation in which our agriculture finds itself. That is one of the major factors of the stagnation now facing agriculture. Those large businesses must be put in their place, and quickly.
Furthermore, a bank of farm products should be created as soon as possible and I congratulate the minister who said he intends to do so. It was pointed out in the Globe and Mail of October 11, 1974. In fact, I would like to ask the minister what has since been done? We need that bank as soon as possible to ensure our national security.
The Minister of Agriculture stated that he was in favour of establishing a world system of food security through large-scale stocking. It is true to maintain that we have no right to consider Canadian agriculture apart while severe starvation is experienced in extensive areas throughout the world.
For all those reasons, we should no longer hear the following in Canada: "Do not produce too much; avoid production or avoid overproduction." Those words were said again recently and it immediately reminded me that the same Liberal government repeated them in 1971 to western grain producers and even paid to prevent them from producing. We see today the fine results: they are disastrous. Madam Speaker, our country has no reserve and eastern farmers must pay excessive prices for grain.
The situation is urgent. Moreover, the country cannot be administered as it was 15 or 20 years ago, when a politician or a minister could allow himself to consider a problem for months and years knowing that one way or another, the problem would solve itself with time. We can no longer say: Time will mend things. On the contrary, it has become obvious that time worsens the situation and heightens the problems. We cannot delay, we must take immediately drastic measures to preserve our agriculture.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-REQUEST FOR INCREASED FUNDS FOR DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it will be difficult for me to answer in two and a half minutes all the things the hon. member raised in his speech this evening. Let me say, first, that in less than two years the government has granted industrial milk producers increases of approximately 40 per cent.
Some of the things the hon. member said this evening have little to do with the question he raised in the House
Adjournment Debate
the other day, and I feel I can add little to what I said when the hon. member opposite raised his question the other day. I must advise him that I am not completely certain what he means when he refers to the need for special subsidies.
I remind all hon. members that there are several important bills before this House which are designed to enable farmers to receive a more stable return for the products they produce. These bills are needed and must pass if we are to see continued expansion in Canadian agriculture. One that I hope receives quick passage tomorrow deals with farm trade. Maybe members could even pass the farm stabilization bill so that we can get on with the business of running agriculture in Canada.
I remind the hon. member that general stabilization is provided under the terms of the Agricultural Stabilization Act. This act provides for a revolving fund of $250 million and can be drawn upon as required to stabilize producers' returns. The revolving fund is then recouped through supplementary estimates.
I note the hon. member's concern about the supply and price of hay. I can advise my colleague opposite that my officials have checked on the situation and are following it closely. Our reports indicate that sufficient supplies are generally available. It does appear that to coax out supplies farmers must pay prices which are above those they are normally accustomed to paying.
I cannot agree that the government should take action at this time to import hay from the United States since there is nothing to stop producers from arranging on their own to buy hay in the United States and transport it to Canada, duty free. Our information is, however, that prices in the United States are the same as or higher than those prevailing in eastern Canada.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUPS-SUGGESTED ACTION TO ENSURE MAIL DELIVERY
PUBLIC SERVICE-STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUPS-SUGGESTED ACTION TO ENSURE MAIL DELIVERY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the disruption of mail service in the Toronto area as well as other parts of Canada is threatening the very existence of the small businessman, an existence which has become a vital part of our overall economy as it is the small businesses that form the backbone of our economic and industrial way of life.
It is the small businessman who has to depend on regular mail delivery to keep his establishment operating on a day to day basis. Without regular mail delivery, there are literally thousands of businesses in the Toronto area alone which are finding it impossible to meet their payrolls, with many of them already laying off employees due to the curtailment of orders being received. They cannot, without regular mail delivery, keep their flow of cash moving and be expected to adhere to their budget requirements.
On top of this, and the sagging economic climate Canadians in general are being asked by the government to accept as a way of life, the Minister of Revenue (Mr. Basford) has the gall to instruct federal sales tax offices to demand of business establishments the delivery of their

February 27, 1975
Adjournment Debate
federal sales taxes at their own expense to the government by any means other than the post office mails.
As if this were not enough, and with a general post office strike a likely possibility in the near future, the national representatives of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers, who were to attend the Joint Senate-House Committee on Employer-Employee Relations in the Public Service of Canada this afternoon, did not attend because, as stated in a brief presented to the committee in their stead, and I quote from that brief:
The responsibility for this decision can be attributed to the recent actions of the Treasury Board of Canada which is trying to use the postal workers to break the strike of the general labour and trades component of the Public Service Alliance of Canada.
Earlier this week the post office, although shut down in Toronto, delivered over one million cheques to old age pensioners and other welfare recipients in that city because many of these individuals could not get by without them. That was indeed a very heart-warming gesture. However, let me assure you that there are many, many small and medium size businesses which cannot get by without regular mail delivery either.
With a continuation of this strike, and others that will inevitably follow unless some immediate alternate course is taken by the government, we will only add to the complete destruction of the economy in this country. It is plain to see that the suggestions I made last week, as well as those made in the memorandum to cabinet by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), relating to the fragmentation of union power should be seriously considered. Let me suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if this permissive government is hesitant in dealing with single public sectors, or is hesitant in asking the post office through the Public Service Alliance of Canada to deliver all business documents along the line welfare cheques were delivered, and surely we cannot be expected to wait for the Finkelman committee to conclude its deliberations, then I believe it is time that serious consideration be given to introducing legislation which would eliminate the right to strike in essential services, but which would instead, for the sake of the working man, establish an automatic annual cost of living increase, with an additional yearly adjustment in the form of a bonus.
It is clear that unions in this country have become more powerful than the federal government, which seems to be becoming weaker. This is obvious from the failure on the part of the government to prosecute individuals taking part in illegal strikes. Although it may be beneficial in the
long run for the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) to go prancing around Europe, it is hard to believe that in these troubled times at home, with growing militancy within the labour force in many sectors of the economy, the Prime Minister of Canada should turn his back on problems which should and must receive the total attention of the head of the government. The example set by the leader of the government will not help matters.
Continued work stoppages of this kind, which last year resulted in the loss of approximately 10 million work days, and are expected to give rise to an even worse situation in 1975, can no longer be tolerated unless Canadians, two-thirds of whom do not belong to unions, are prepared to live in conditions of economic disaster.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gaston Clermont (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUPS-SUGGESTED ACTION TO ENSURE MAIL DELIVERY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the disruption of postal service in the Toronto area results from the current General Labour and Trades strike. Members of that union who maintain equipment and vehicles in the Post Office in Toronto are engaging in a lawful strike, and have set up picket lines at certain postal installations in Toronto and elsewhere.
Treasury Board has been informed that a number of mail service couriers who work for the Post Office Department have refused to cross the picket lines. This has resulted in internal transportation facilities not being available to the Post Office in Toronto. The ultimate effect is that mail cannot be delivered to or from the postal processing facilities, thus disruption and eventually causing the shut-down of the Post Office in Toronto.
Picket lines are not intended to deny people rightful access to buildings and installations. Employees who do not have the right to strike and who work in buildings picketed by striking GL and T employees have an obligation and a right to report for work and perform their assigned duties.
With respect to claims by employees that they have attempted to cross picket lines but have been unable to do so because of threats or intimidation, an employee should be considered on duty only where it is clear that an attempt was made to cross the picket line, and the employee concerned was either barred from entry or threatened with violence by a member of the picket.
The answer lies not in the solution proposed by the hon. member for High Park-Humber Valley (Mr. Jelinek) but in the return to work at the Toronto Post Office of all employees who do not have the lawful right to strike so that the postal service may be restored to the public.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.42 p.m.

Friday, February 28, 1975
